data.title: Commentary: Black Friday is here, but what’s behind our need to chase bargains?
data.description: CARDIFF: Black Friday is a highly successful US export. The retail strategy designed to kickstart festive shopping has become a global phenomenon. But are the hype and the pressure (and the occasional fight over electrical hardware) worth it? After all, most products on offer during Black Friday are available at the same price (or even less) at other times of the year. So why do so many people still join in? Here are some of the marketing tricks and psychological drivers that help to explain the appeal of Black Friday.  MARKETING PUSH Offers that exist for a limited time period are among the oldest retail marketing tricks in the book. And there is plenty of research which shows that they reliably increase a shopper’s intention to buy. If we think a deal will disappear after Black Friday, the fear of missing out on a bargain can push us towards buying that air fryer or scented candle. Or we might buy it to avoid the potential feelings of regret that may come if we don’t. Price tags also have a big effect. Psychologists have shown that when making value judgments, the first number we see disproportionately shapes how we evaluate subsequent numbers. So when a price tag reads: “"Was £100 (US$131)! Now £60!”, the £100 figure is the one we latch on to. This makes £60 feel like a £40 saving rather than a £60 expense, even if the item was never really worth £100 in the first place. CONSUMER PULL While many people will be aware of these kinds of retail marketing tricks, they will still willingly participate in Black Friday. This may be partly due to its timing, but also to the psychological rewards that shopping could offer. In the northern hemisphere at least, Black Friday coincides with the “winter blues”, potentially offering a source of excitement as the days get colder and darker. We may also shop to improve our mood with a little “retail therapy”.One explanation for the effectiveness of retail therapy is that negative emotions often come from situations we cannot change. Making choices about what we want and then buying those things might help us to restore a feeling of personal control. Another reason is that buying generally might bring more positive than negative emotions. But studies have also shown that the temporary uplift from purchasing does not last as long as we often think it will. Landing a bargain can also make us feel good about ourselves. Being a “smart shopper” has been linked to a personal sense of achievement and pride when we secure a good deal. Buying things at a (genuine) discount can also demonstrate competence and good financial management to others. But that is not the only social appeal of Black Friday. Even the most independently minded consumer can be influenced by what other people do. And engaging in an activity at the same time as others, even among strangers, can temporarily enhance feelings of social connection.WHAT ARE WE REALLY BUYING? Despite the thrill of a bargain, or joining in with a commercial social event, what feels rewarding in the moment may not necessarily contribute to our longer-term wellbeing. Research in consumption has shown that spending money on things that fit our personality or that help us with personal goals might be a good idea. For example, an extrovert or someone looking to develop new connections will probably benefit more from spending money on social activities than buying a discounted item. But why we buy is as important as what we buy. In a recent study, my colleagues and I found that spending money in response to social pressure, to gain status or to seek others’ approval was linked to low wellbeing. So even experiences do not always bring more happiness. Our expectations can also mislead us. In another study I worked on, my colleagues and I found that people thought that buying new clothes would make them feel better about themselves than buying second-hand clothes. But it turned out that buying old and new clothes had pretty much the same effect. More broadly, research shows that focusing on economic gains and consumption brings a lower sense of wellbeing and is detrimental to our personal relationships. In contrast, choosing to live more simply or buying less is consistently linked with greater wellbeing. People who become less focused on material goals tend to become happier over time. So perhaps Black Friday should not simply be about how much money we are saving or how much temporary joy our purchases might bring us. Maybe it’s a time to reflect on what we gain from spending more money on more stuff, and whether there might be more sustainable and lasting alternatives. Olaya Moldes Andres is Senior Lecturer in Consumer Behaviour at Cardiff University. This commentary first appeared on The Conversation.

data.title: Japan's JERA enters talks with Anthropic, Meta to build data centres, Nikkei reports
data.description: Nov 27 : Japan's largest power generator, JERA, has entered into talks with Anthropic, Meta, and other US tech giants to build data centers near power plants in the Tokyo area, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Friday. JERA Global CEO and Chair Yukio Kani said in a recent interview that the energy group is also in discussions with Amazon, Microsoft and Google, Nikkei reported. JERA announced a partnership with Dell Technologies and UK-based AI infrastructure developer RHAELM in October to accelerate the development of artificial intelligence infrastructure in Japan. They signed a memorandum of understanding to develop a standardised model for building AI infrastructure on a national scale, starting with a $15 billion hyperscale data centre in Chiba, near Tokyo. A JERA spokesperson said RHAELM is in charge of marketing and the company had been told that RHAELM is in talks with multiple hyperscalers. RHAELM was not immediately available for comment. Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Google did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

data.title: SAP reportedly considering at least 10,000 job cuts in AI restructuring
data.description: German software giant SAP is considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs in an AI-driven restructuring, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday (Nov 26), citing people familiar with the matter. The restructuring would affect at least 9 per cent of SAP's global workforce, Bloomberg said, adding that the total number of job cuts could change after labour negotiations. SAP, Europe's most valuable tech company, declined to commment. The plans have yet to be discussed with employee representatives, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. SAP joins a growing list of major German companies weighing workforce reductions after automakers including Volkswagen and BMW have announced deep cuts as they grapple with sluggish demand and increasing competition from China, reported Financial Times.  US technology rivals including Microsoft , Oracle and Salesforce have also announced thousands of job cuts in recent months, citing AI-driven efficiencies and efforts to cut costs.  If implemented, the plan would mark SAP's second major round of layoffs in about two years.  The software giant slashed 10,000 jobs in a major restructuring in 2024, though subsequent hiring has pushed its total headcount back up to about 113,000, according to Financial Times.

data.title: Japan Tobacco shares climb on talk that it may be part of Imperial Brands takeover
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Japan Tobacco shares rose on Friday following a report that it was considering partnering on a multibillion-dollar takeover of British cigarette maker Imperial Brands — potentially one of the largest in the industry's history. A day earlier, US tobacco group Altria said it was considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and was discussing a deal involving acquiring part of its business with another party. Tokyo-based JT is considering teaming up with a partner, Bloomberg News reported. JT declined to comment on the report. In morning trade, JT shares were up 3.6 per cent, outperforming a 1 per cent gain for Japan's benchmark TOPIX index. The potential deal reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth avenues as smoking rates fall — a decline that has been difficult to completely offset with newer nicotine products. Shares in Imperial, which said it had not received an approach but whose board would consider any proposal, jumped 13.8 per cent on Thursday, valuing it at £25.90 billion ($34 billion). Imperial would give a buyer a portfolio of established cigarette brands including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, which are sold in more than 100 markets. "This deal would make a lot of sense for both (Altria) and JT, in our view, while we believe the deal could be done without impacting the current credit ratings of either name," BTIG analyst Owen Bennett said in a note. JT, whose brands include Camel, Benson & Hedges and the Ploom heated tobacco device range, could acquire assets from Imperial Brands in the US, Africa and the Middle East, Bennett said. JT has been expanding its US tobacco business, particularly in cheaper labels that have been winning market share. A deal could "turn JT into a sizeable, diversified, and value-rational 3rd-place US competitor with cost synergy potential," Jefferies analyst Andrei Andon-Ionita said in a note. A takeover by JT of Imperial's US business should avoid antitrust issues given a combined value share of 14 per cent, smaller than Altria and British American Tobacco, he said. In recent years, JT has done deals in countries such as Bangladesh, the Philippines and Ethiopia. JT, whose shareholders include the Japanese government, said last week it would record an $8.7 billion loss after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries when ​President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure this month. That seizure will continue to impede any share gains for Japan Tobacco, said Tatsunori Kawai, chief strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ eSmart Securities.

data.title: BOJ calls for safeguards against digital money, AI risks
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Global policymakers must strengthen defences against financial stability and cybersecurity risks posed by the emergence of new forms of digital money and financial infrastructure, Bank of Japan Executive Director Kazushige Kamiyama said on Friday. New forms of digital money, such as stablecoins and tokenised deposits, are likely to co-exist and interact, which poses fresh challenges for policymakers such as ensuring the diversity does not create unnecessary fragmentation or undermine financial stability, he said. The growing use of AI also brings fresh cybersecurity risks, requiring authorities and institutions to strengthen their defences against the growing ability of AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, Kamiyama said. "My central message is that technological innovation offers significant opportunities to improve money and payments, but innovation must go hand in hand with trust," Kamiyama said in a speech delivered to the International Monetary Fund's seminar on digital money and payments in Tokyo. "Central bank money will continue to play a fundamental role as the anchor of trust in the monetary system," he said.

data.title: Chinese industrial profit rises 16% in January-October
data.description: BEIJING, Nov 27 : Profit at Chinese industrial firms rose 16 per cent in the first 10 months of this year over the corresponding period last year, official data showed on Friday. The increase quickened from 15.5 per cent in the January-September period, showed data from the National Bureau of Statistics. Industrial profit figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($3 million) from main operations. ($1 = 6.6722 Chinese yuan)

data.title: Dollar lingers near 22-month peak as AI worries simmer
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : The US dollar hovered below a 22-month peak in holiday-thinned trading on Friday, with traders looking to equity markets for clues on direction as doubts about the AI trade triggers heightened volatility. The dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of six peers, was steady at 103.81, at the end of a week that saw it pop to the highest level since March of last year at 104.53 on Monday only to erase those gains a day later. For the week, the index is currently flat. The US currency edged up 0.1 per cent to 159.355 yen early in Friday's Asian session, and also strengthened slightly to 0.83455 Swiss franc. The euro was little changed at $1.0964 and sterling eased slightly to $1.3099. The risk-sensitive Aussie dollar weakened a touch to $0.6631, after dipping to a one-year low of $0.6559 on Wednesday. "All eyes are on whether the downtrend in AI-related stocks will turn around," Mizuho analysts wrote in a client note. A recovery could see currencies such as the Aussie and high-yielding Mexican peso bounce back, while renewed selling would likely see those currencies under additional pressure, they said. The US currency has been supported by expectations for Federal Reserve policy tightening with traders seeing a quarter-point interest rate hike on December 9 as a near certainty, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. Hotter-than-expected US core personal consumption expenditures inflation in October, a sharp upward revision to third-quarter gross domestic product and a Federal Reserve survey showing continued economic growth and sticky inflation also have traders confident of an additional hike by around April. The dollar index has risen about 5.7 per cent so far in 2026, with only a month left in the year. "The USD looks to be on a stronger-for-longer path than previously expected," NAB strategists wrote in a research report. However, "given its rapid rise, we see limited scope for further gains," they added.

data.title: Binance lifts withdrawal suspension after $6.3 billion crypto heist

data.title: US Marlboro maker Altria explores Imperial cash bid, possible carve-up
data.description: Nov 26 : US tobacco group Altria said on Thursday it was considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and was discussing a deal involving part of the British tobacco group's business with another party, while Japan Tobacco was also reported to be weighing a bid. The moves potentially set the stage for one of the largest deals in tobacco industry history, combining three companies that together account for a significant share of the global cigarette market. Shares in London-listed Imperial jumped 13.8 per cent to 3,449 pence, giving it a market value of £25.90 billion ($33.93 billion). Depending on the structure of the deal, Altria could overtake British American Tobacco as the world's second-most valuable listed tobacco company, behind US Philip Morris International. Bloomberg News reported earlier on Thursday that Japan Tobacco was evaluating a potential acquisition of Imperial Brands, possibly with a partner, splitting up its assets around the world, citing people familiar with the matter. Analysts said a joint US-Japanese takeover could swerve antitrust objections and solve strategic challenges. The potential deal reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth avenues as smoking rates fall, and some struggle to compensate with newer nicotine products. Imperial said it had not had any discussions with, or received any approach from, Altria or a third party. "The Board is clear in its duty of aiming to maximise shareholder value and will consider any proposal, should one be made," it said in a statement. Japan Tobacco declined to comment on Bloomberg's report. IMPERIAL'S APPEAL TO BUYERS Imperial would give any buyer a portfolio of established cigarette brands spanning Europe and the United States, including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, sold in more than 100 markets. A deal could mark a return to international cigarette sales for Altria, two decades after it spun off its international division to focus on the United States. That move created Philip Morris International. Altria has not sold cigarettes or most other products outside the US since, leaving it more exposed than rivals to several key challenges in that market. Altria has a market value of $126.89 billion, while Japan Tobacco, which sells brands including Camel and Benson & Hedges in more than 130 markets, is valued at roughly $69.45 billion. A deal for Imperial Brands would rank among the largest recent acquisitions of a British company by an overseas buyer. London-listed firms have become attractive acquisition targets in recent years due to depressed valuations compared to their rivals listed on other European or US exchanges. Imperial Brands trades at just 8.3 times forward earnings compared with 12.6 times for Altria and 17.7 times for Japan Tobacco, LSEG data showed. The mega-deal would add to this year's global M&A haul, which has been expected by bankers to rival the record-breaking 2021 total even after a pullback in dealmaking in the wake of rising rates. SEARCHING FOR GROWTH Japan Tobacco, Altria and Imperial Brands have all lagged behind rivals such as PMI and British American Tobacco in expanding beyond traditional tobacco, with past efforts yielding mixed results. "Imperial and to a lesser extent (Japan Tobacco) and Altria are in a tough strategic spot, without the financial firepower to properly compete with (PMI and BAT) as the nicotine industry transitions from legacy cigarettes," Callum Elliott, analyst at Bernstein, said in a note. Last week, Imperial Brands, which makes Winston cigarettes, announced plans to cut up to 4,600 jobs, or nearly a fifth of its workforce. Altria and Japan Tobacco already have ties, having launched a joint venture in 2022 to grow newer product lines. Japan Tobacco has also been expanding its US tobacco business, particularly in cheaper labels that have been winning market share - a trend that has benefited Imperial's brands. Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until December 24 to make a firm offer or walk away. ($1 = 0.7634 pounds) ($1 = 159.1700 yen)

data.title: EU may vote on authorising Tesla assisted-driving system at Dec 15 meeting
data.description: STOCKHOLM, Nov 26 : A meeting of European Union countries on December 15 on whether to approve Tesla's assisted-driving system across the bloc may include a formal vote by member states on approval, according to a draft agenda published by the European Commission. Reuters reported on Wednesday that a meeting where the technology would be discussed had been postponed to December 15. On Thursday, in a draft agenda published for the meeting, the Commission explicitly raises the possibility of a vote for the first time, saying EU countries will further examine the Dutch request to grant type approval for the system "with possible vote".  The vote is a key step in Tesla's effort to roll out the technology across Europe, with nearly a dozen countries having followed the Dutch lead. But ​EU-wide approval requires ⁠backing from at least 15 of the bloc's 27 member states representing 65 per cent of its ​population.

data.title: Polish defence ministry to sign agreement with Palantir on Friday
data.description: WARSAW, Nov 26 : Poland's defence ministry will sign an agreement with Palantir Technologies Inc. on Friday to buy software that uses artificial intelligence to support decision-making processes, the ministry said on Thursday. • No other details of the agreement were provided in a statement • Poland started cooperation with Palantir in 2025, when it signed a memorandum of understanding covering artificial intelligence, information technology, and cybersecurity

data.title: Core inflation in Tokyo hits 16-month high, bolsters case for BOJ hike
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Annual core inflation in Japan's capital accelerated in November at the fastest pace in 16 months, highlighting mounting price pressure and bolstering the case for an interest rate hike as soon as next month. The data, widely regarded as a leading indicator of nationwide trends, will be among factors the Bank of Japan scrutinises in deciding whether to raise interest rates at its next two-day policy meeting ending on December 18. The core consumer price index, which includes prices of fuel but not fresh food, in Tokyo rose 2.9 per cent in November from a year earlier, data showed on Friday, compared with the median market forecast of 3.0 per cent. It followed a 2.6 per cent gain in October and marked the fastest year-on-year rise since July 2025. Core inflation thus stayed above the BOJ's 2 per cent target for three straight months, cementing the case for further hikes. While the increase was driven partly by an end to government utility subsidies, prices rose for a broad range of goods and services including food, daily necessities and hotel charges. "Core consumer inflation is expected to accelerate due to rising energy prices from the Middle East conflict and ensuing second-round effects," said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "If the current market instability stemming from concern over the AI and chip outlook persists, there's a chance the BOJ may forgo a rate hike in December. But our baseline projection is for the BOJ to proceed with one next month," he said. An index stripping away the effect of volatile fresh food and fuel prices, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a more accurate gauge of trend inflation, rose 2.5 per cent in November after a 2.6 per cent gain in October, the data showed. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import costs from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes seen in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady in October, but said underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target and signalled its readiness to continue hiking rates to prevent price growth from accelerating too much. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another hike by end-March. Many see the terminal rate at around 1.75 per cent or 2.0 per cent. Hawkish BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said on Thursday the central bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by accelerating the pace of rate hikes.
